entries.652fa28fd4d89278e665638fc932a093861010ee: <div sID="gen2481" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Lev.18" sID="Lev.18"/> <div eID="gen2481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2482" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2483" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general law against all conformity to the corrupt usages of the heathen, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.1-Lev.18.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Particular laws, 1. Against incest, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.6-Lev.18.18">ver. 6-18</reference>. 2. Against beastly lusts, and barbarous idolatries, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.19-Lev.18.23">ver. 19-23</reference>. III. The enforcement of these laws from the ruin of the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.24-Lev.18.30">ver. 24-30</reference>.
entries.ab6f04e9c17beef030bd0d7f9431e825554fd3fc: <div eID="gen2483" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2482" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against Idolatrous Practices. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2484" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, I am the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">3</hi> After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do: and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do: neither shall ye walk in their ordinances. <hi type="super">4</hi> Ye shall do my judgments, and keep mine ordinances, to walk therein: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">5</hi> Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen2484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2485" type="x-p"/> After divers ceremonial institutions, God here returns to the enforcement of moral precepts. The former are still of use to us as types, the latter still binding as laws. We have here, 1. The sacred authority by which these laws are enacted: <hi type="italic">I am the Lord your God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.4">4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.30">30</reference>), and <hi type="italic">I am the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.5-Lev.18.6">v. 5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">21</reference>. "The Lord, who has a right to rule all; your God, who has a peculiar right to rule you." Jehovah is the fountain of being, and therefore the fountain of power, whose we are, whom we are bound to serve, and who is able to punish all disobedience. "Your God to whom you have consented, in whom you are happy, to whom you lie under the highest obligations imaginable, and to whom you are accountable." 2. A strict caution to take heed of retaining the relics of the idolatries of Egypt, where they had dwelt, and of receiving the infection of the idolatries of Canaan, whither they were now going, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.3">v. 3</reference>. Now that God was by Moses teaching them his ordinances there was <hi type="italic">aliquid dediscendum—something to be unlearned,</hi> which they had sucked in with their milk in Egypt, a country noted for idolatry: <hi type="italic">You shall not do after the doings of the land of Egypt.</hi> It would be the greatest absurdity in itself to retain such an affection for their house of bondage as to be governed in their devotions by the usages of it, and the greatest ingratitude to God, who had so wonderfully and graciously delivered them. Nay, as if governed by a spirit of contradiction, they would be in danger, even after they had received these ordinances of God, of admitting the wicked usages of the Canaanites and of inheriting their vices with their land. Of this danger they are here warned, <hi type="italic">You shall not walk in their ordinances.</hi> Such a tyrant is custom that their practices are called <hi type="italic">ordinances,</hi> and they became rivals even with God's ordinances, and God's professing people were in danger of receiving law from them. 3. A solemn charge to them to <hi type="italic">keep God's judgments, statutes, and ordinances,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.4-Lev.18.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. To this charge, and many similar ones, David seems to refer in the many prayers and professions he makes relating to God's laws in the <reference osisRef="Ps.119">119th Psalm</reference>. Observe here, (1.) The great rule of our obedience—God's statutes and judgments. These we must <hi type="italic">keep to walk therein.</hi> We must keep them in our books, and keep them in our hands, that we may practise them in our hearts and lives. <hi type="italic">Remember God's commandments to do them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.18">Ps. ciii. 18</reference>. We must keep in them as our way to travel in, keep to them as our rule to work by, keep them as our treasure, as the apple of our eye, with the utmost care and value. (2.) The great advantage of our obedience: <hi type="italic">Which if a man do, he shall live in them,</hi> that is, "he shall be happy here and hereafter." We have reason to thank God, [1.] That this is still in force as a promise, with a very favourable construction of the condition. If we keep God's commandments in sincerity, though we come short of sinless perfection, we shall find that the way of duty is the way of comfort, and will be the way to happiness. Godliness has the <hi type="italic">promise of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1 Tim. iv. 8</reference>. Wisdom has said, <hi type="italic">Keep my commandments and live:</hi> and <hi type="italic">if through the Spirit we mortify the deeds of the body</hi> (which are to us as the usages of Egypt were to Israel) <hi type="italic">we shall live.</hi> [2.] That it is not so in force in the nature of a covenant as that the least transgression shall for ever exclude us from this life. The apostle quotes this twice as opposite to the faith which the gospel reveals. It is the description of the <hi type="italic">righteousness which is by the law, the man that doeth them shall live</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en autois</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">in them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.5">Rom. x. 5</reference>), and is urged to prove that <hi type="italic">the law is not of faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">Gal. iii. 12</reference>. The alteration which the gospel has made is in the last word: still <hi type="italic">the man that does them shall live,</hi> but not live <hi type="italic">in them;</hi> for the law could not give life, because we could not perfectly keep it; it was <hi type="italic">weak through the flesh,</hi> not in itself; but now <hi type="italic">the man that does them</hi> shall <hi type="italic">live by the faith of the Son of God.</hi> He shall owe his life to the grace of Christ, and not to the merit of his own works; see <reference osisRef="Gal.3.21-Gal.3.22">Gal. iii. 21, 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">The just shall live,</hi> but they shall live <hi type="italic">by faith,</hi> by virtue of their union with Christ, who is their life.
entries.9d428d789088b7f280fbd412f51e22cd4f1acf77: <div eID="gen2485" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Incest Defined and Forbidden; Against Marrying Near Relations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2486" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover <hi type="italic">their</hi> nakedness: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> The nakedness of thy father, or the nakedness of thy mother, shalt thou not uncover: she <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy mother; thou shalt not uncover her nakedness. <hi type="super">8</hi> The nakedness of thy father's wife shalt thou not uncover: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy father's nakedness. <hi type="super">9</hi> The nakedness of thy sister, the daughter of thy father, or daughter of thy mother, <hi type="italic">whether she be</hi> born at home, or born abroad, <hi type="italic">even</hi> their nakedness thou shalt not uncover. <hi type="super">10</hi> The nakedness of thy son's daughter, or of thy daughter's daughter, <hi type="italic">even</hi> their nakedness thou shalt not uncover: for theirs <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine own nakedness. <hi type="super">11</hi> The nakedness of thy father's wife's daughter, begotten of thy father, she <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy sister, thou shalt not uncover her nakedness. <hi type="super">12</hi> Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister: she <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy father's near kinswoman. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy mother's sister: for she <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy mother's near kinswoman. 14 Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's brother, thou shalt not approach to his wife: she <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine aunt. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy daughter in law: she <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy son's wife; thou shalt not uncover her nakedness. <hi type="super">16</hi> Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy brother's nakedness. <hi type="super">17</hi> Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; <hi type="italic">for</hi> they <hi type="italic">are</hi> her near kinswomen: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> wickedness. <hi type="super">18</hi> Neither shalt thou take a wife to her sister, to vex <hi type="italic">her,</hi> to uncover her nakedness, beside the other in her life <hi type="italic">time.</hi> <div eID="gen2486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2487" type="x-p"/> These laws relate to the seventh commandment, and, no doubt, are obligatory on us under the gospel, for they are consonant to the very light and law of nature: one of the articles, that of a man's having his father's wife, the apostle speaks of as a sin <hi type="italic">not so much as named among the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1 Cor. v. 1</reference>. Though some of the incests here forbidden were practised by some particular persons among the heathen, yet they were disallowed and detested, unless among those nations who had become barbarous, and were quite given up to vile affections. Observe, <div eID="gen2487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2488" type="x-p"/> I. That which is forbidden as to the relations here specified is <hi type="italic">approaching to them to uncover their nakedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.6">v. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen2488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2489" type="x-p"/> 1. It is chiefly intended to forbid the marrying of any of these relations. Marriage is a divine institution; this and the sabbath, the eldest of all, of equal standing with man upon the earth: it is intended for the comfort of human life, and the decent and honourable propagation of the human race, such as became the dignity of man's nature above that of the beasts. It is <hi type="italic">honourable in all,</hi> and these laws are for the support of the honour of it. It was requisite that a divine ordinance should be subject to divine rules and restraints, especially because it concerns a thing wherein the corrupt nature of man is as apt as in any thing to be wilful and impetuous in its desires, and impatient of check. Yet these prohibitions, besides their being enacted by an incontestable authority, are in themselves highly reasonable and equitable. (1.) By marriage two were to become one flesh, therefore those that before were in a sense one flesh by nature could not, without the greatest absurdity, become one flesh by institution; for the institution was designed to unite those who before were not united. (2.) Marriage puts an equality between husband and wife. "Is she not thy companion taken out of thy side?" Therefore, if those who before were superior and inferior should intermarry (which is the case in most of the instances here laid down), the order of nature would be taken away by a positive institution, which must by no means be allowed. The inequality between master and servant, noble and ignoble, is founded in consent and custom, and there is no harm done if that be taken away by the equality of marriage; but the inequality between parents and children, uncles and nieces, aunts and nephews, either by blood or marriage, is founded in nature, and is therefore perpetual, and cannot without confusion be taken away by the equality of marriage, the institution of which, though ancient, is subsequent to the order of nature. (3.) No relations that are equals are forbidden, except brothers and sisters, by the whole blood or half blood, or by marriage; and in this there is not the same natural absurdity as in the former, for Adam's sons must of necessity have married their own sisters; but it was requisite that it should be made by a positive law unlawful and detestable, for the preventing of sinful familiarities between those that in the days of their youth are supposed to live in a house together, and yet cannot intermarry without defeating one of the intentions of marriage, which is the enlargement of friendship and interest. If every man married his own sister (as they would be apt to do from generation to generation if it were lawful), each family would be a world to itself, and it would be forgotten that <hi type="italic">we are members one of another.</hi> It is certain that this has always been looked upon by the more sober heathen as a most infamous and abominable thing; and those who had not this law yet were herein a law to themselves. The making use of the ordinance of marriage for the patronizing of incestuous mixtures is so far from justifying them, or extenuating their guilt, that it adds the guilt of profaning an ordinance of God, and prostituting that to the vilest of purposes which was instituted for the noblest ends. But, <div eID="gen2489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2490" type="x-p"/> 2. Uncleanness, committed with any of these relations out of marriage, is likewise, without doubt, forbidden here, and no less intended than the former: as also all lascivious carriage, wanton dalliance, and every thing that has the appearance of this evil. Relations must love one another, and are to have free and familiar converse with each other, but it must be with all purity; and the less it is suspected of evil by others the more care ought the persons themselves to take that <hi type="italic">Satan do not get advantage against them,</hi> for he is a very subtle enemy, and seeks all occasions against us. <div eID="gen2490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2491" type="x-p"/> II. The relations forbidden are most of them plainly described; and it is generally laid down as a rule that what relations of a man's own he is bound up from marrying the same relations of his wife he is likewise forbidden to marry, for they two are one. That law which forbids marrying a brother's wife (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.16">v. 16</reference>) had an exception peculiar to the Jewish state, that, if a man died without issue, his brother or next of kin should marry the widow, and raise up seed to the deceased (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.5">Deut. xxv. 5</reference>), for reasons which held good only in that commonwealth; and therefore now that those reasons have ceased the exception ceases, and the law is in force, that a man must in no case marry his brother's widow. That article (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.18">v. 18</reference>) which forbids a man to <hi type="italic">take a wife to her sister</hi> supposes a connivance at polygamy, as some other laws then did (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Exod. xxi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.15">Deut. xxi. 15</reference>), but forbids a man's marrying two sisters, as Jacob did, because between those who had before been equal there would be apt to arise greater jealousies and animosities than between wives that were not so nearly related. If the sister of the wife be taken for the concubine, or secondary wife, nothing can be more vexing in her life, or as long as she lives.
entries.993df9ee3b559e94b991c00845e9aa17c602d246: <div eID="gen2491" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Laws against Iniquity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Also thou shalt not approach unto a woman to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is put apart for her uncleanness. <hi type="super">20</hi> Moreover thou shalt not lie carnally with thy neighbour's wife, to defile thyself with her. <hi type="super">21</hi> And thou shalt not let any of thy seed pass through <hi type="italic">the fire</hi> to Molech, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">22</hi> Thou shalt not lie with mankind, as with womankind: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> abomination. 23 Neither shalt thou lie with any beast to defile thyself therewith: neither shall any woman stand before a beast to lie down thereto: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> confusion. <hi type="super">24</hi> Defile not ye yourselves in any of these things: for in all these the nations are defiled which I cast out before you: <hi type="super">25</hi> And the land is defiled: therefore I do visit the iniquity thereof upon it, and the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants. <hi type="super">26</hi> Ye shall therefore keep my statutes and my judgments, and shall not commit <hi type="italic">any</hi> of these abominations; <hi type="italic">neither</hi> any of your own nation, nor any stranger that sojourneth among you: <hi type="super">27</hi> (For all these abominations have the men of the land done, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> before you, and the land is defiled;) <hi type="super">28</hi> That the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that <hi type="italic">were</hi> before you. <hi type="super">29</hi> For whosoever shall commit any of these abominations, even the souls that commit <hi type="italic">them</hi> shall be cut off from among their people. <hi type="super">30</hi> Therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance, that <hi type="italic">ye</hi> commit not <hi type="italic">any one</hi> of these abominable customs, which were committed before you, and that ye defile not yourselves therein: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <div eID="gen2492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2493" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A law to preserve the honour of the marriage-bed, that it should not be unseasonably used (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.19">v. 19</reference>), nor invaded by an adulterer, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.20">v. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen2493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2494" type="x-p"/> II. A law against that which was the most unnatural idolatry, causing their children to <hi type="italic">pass through the fire to Moloch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">v. 21</reference>. Moloch (as some think) was the idol in and by which they worshipped the sun, that great fire of the world; and therefore in the worship of it they made their own children either sacrifices to this idol, burning them to death before it, or devotees to it, causing them to pass between two fires, as some think, or to be thrown through one, to the honour of this pretended deity, imagining that the consecrating of but one of their children in this manner to Moloch would procure good fortune for all the rest of their children. Did idolaters thus give their own children to false gods, and shall we think any thing too dear to be dedicated to, or to be parted with for, the true God? See how this sin of Israel (which they were afterwards guilty of, notwithstanding this law) is aggravated by the relation which they and their children stood in to God. <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.20">Ezek. xvi. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou hast taken thy sons and thy daughters, whom thou hast borne unto me, and these thou hast sacrificed.</hi> Therefore it is here called <hi type="italic">profaning the name of their</hi> God; for it looked as if they thought they were under greater obligations to Moloch than to Jehovah; for to him they offered their cattle only, but to Moloch their children. <div eID="gen2494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2495" type="x-p"/> III. A law against unnatural lusts, sodomy and bestiality, sins not to be named nor thought of without the utmost abhorrence imaginable, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.22-Lev.18.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. Other sins level men with the beasts, but these sink them much lower. That ever there should have been occasion for the making of these laws, and that since they are published they should ever have been broken, is the perpetual reproach and scandal of human nature; and the giving of men up to these vile affections was frequently the punishment of their idolatries; so the apostle shows, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Rom. i. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen2495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2496" type="x-p"/> IV. Arguments against these and the like abominable wickednesses. He that has an indisputable right to command us, yet because he will deal with us as men, and <hi type="italic">draw with the cords of a man,</hi> condescends to reason with us. 1. Sinners defile themselves with these abominations: <hi type="italic">Defile not yourselves in any of these things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.24">v. 24</reference>. All sin is defiling to the conscience, but these are sins that have a peculiar turpitude in them. Our heavenly Father, in kindness to us, requires of us that we keep ourselves clean, and do not wallow in the dirt. 2. <hi type="italic">The souls that commit them shall be cut off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.29">v. 29</reference>. And justly; for, <hi type="italic">if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">1 Cor. iii. 17</reference>. Fleshly lusts war against the soul, and will certainly be the ruin of it if God's mercy and grace prevent not. 3. <hi type="italic">The land is defiled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.25">v. 25</reference>. If such wickednesses as these be practised and connived at, the land is thereby made unfit to have God's tabernacle in it, and the pure and holy God will withdraw the tokens of his gracious presence from it. It is also rendered unwholesome to the inhabitants, who are hereby infected with sin and exposed to plagues and it is really nauseous and loathsome to all good men in it, as the wickedness of Sodom was to the soul of righteous Lot. 4. These have been the abominations of the former inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.24">v. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.27">27</reference>. Therefore it was necessary that these laws should be made, as antidotes and preservatives from the plague are necessary when we go into an infected place. And therefore they should not practise any such things, because the nations that had practised them now lay under the curse of God, and were shortly to fall by the sword of Israel. They could not but be sensible how odious those people had made themselves who wallowed in this mire, and how they stank in the nostrils of all good men; and shall a people sanctified and dignified as Israel was make themselves thus vile? When we observe how ill sin looks in others we should use this as an argument with ourselves with the utmost care and caution to preserve our purity. 5. For these and the like sins the Canaanites were to be destroyed; these filled the measure of the Amorites' iniquity (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Gen. xv. 16</reference>), and brought down that destruction of so many populous kingdoms which the Israelites were now shortly to be not only the spectators, but the instruments of: <hi type="italic">Therefore I do visit the iniquity thereof upon it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.25">v. 25</reference>. Note, The tremendous judgments of God, executed on those that are daringly profane and atheistical, are intended as warnings to those who profess religion to take heed of every thing that has the least appearance of, or tendency towards, profaneness or atheism. Even the ruin of the Canaanites is an admonition to the Israelites not to do like them. Nay, to show that not only the Creator is provoked, but the creation burdened, by such abominations as these, it is added (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.25">v. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">The land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants.</hi> The very ground they went upon did, as it were, groan under them, and was sick of them, and not easy till it had discharged itself of these <hi type="italic">enemies of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa. i. 24</reference>. This bespeaks the extreme loathsomeness of sin; sinful man indeed <hi type="italic">drinks in iniquity like water,</hi> but the harmless part of the creation even heaves at it, and rises against it. Many a house and many a town have spued out the wicked inhabitants, as it were, with abhorrence, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.16">Rev. iii. 16</reference>. Therefore take heed, saith God, <hi type="italic">that the land spue not you out also,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">v. 28</reference>. It was secured to them, and entailed upon them, and yet they must expect that, if they made the vices of the Canaanites their own, with their land their fate would be the same. Note, Wicked Israelites are as abominable to God as wicked Canaanites, and more so, and will be as soon spued out, or sooner. Such a warning as was here given to the Israelites is given by the apostle to the Gentile converts, with reference to the rejected Jews, in whose room they were substituted (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.19">Rom. xi. 19</reference>, &c.); they must take heed of falling <hi type="italic">after the same example of unbelief,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.11">Heb. iv. 11</reference>. Apply it more generally; and let it deter us effectually from all sinful courses to consider how many they have been the ruin of. Lay the ear of faith to the gates of the bottomless pit, and hear the doleful shrieks and outcries of damned sinners, whom earth has spued out and hell has swallowed, that find themselves undone, for ever undone, by sin; and tremble lest this be your portion at last. God's threatenings and judgments should frighten us from sin. <div eID="gen2496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2497" type="x-p"/> V. The chapter concludes with a sovereign antidote against this infection: <hi type="italic">Therefore you shall keep my ordinance that you commit not any one of these abominable customs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.18.30">v. 30</reference>. This is the remedy prescribed. Note, 1. Sinful customs are abominable customs, and their being common and fashionable does not make them at all the less abominable nor should we the less abominate them, but the more; because the more customary they are the more dangerous they are. 2. It is of pernicious consequence to admit and allow of any one sinful custom, because one will make way for many, <hi type="italic">Uno absurdo dato, mille sequuntur—Admit but a single absurdity, you invite a thousand.</hi> The way of sin is downhill. 3. A close and constant adherence to God's ordinances is the most effectual preservative from the infection of gross sin. The more we taste of the sweetness and feel of the power of holy ordinances the less inclination we shall have to the forbidden pleasures of sinners' abominable customs. It is the grace of God only that will secure us, and that grace is to be expected only in the use of the means of grace. Nor does God ever leave any to their own hearts' lusts till they have first left him and his institutions.  <chapter eID="Lev.18"/> <div eID="gen2497" type="x-p"/>

entries.5003de8da9b6c23600efaa804bd5d6b10b99aebf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1122"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.18.1-Lev.18.30">Le 18:1-30</reference>. Unlawful Marriages.</title> <div sID="gen1540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1122"/><hi type="bold">2-4. I am the Lord your God--</hi>This renewed mention of the divine sovereignty over the Israelites was intended to bear particularly on some laws that were widely different from the social customs that obtained both in Egypt and Canaan; for the enormities, which the laws enumerated in this chapter were intended to put down, were freely practised or publicly sanctioned in both of those countries; and, indeed, the extermination of the ancient Canaanites is described as owing to the abominations with which they had polluted the land. <div eID="gen1540" type="x-p"/>
entries.6bd05d70e71c222de3cb33e99c01a543d1c89169: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1123"/><div sID="gen1541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1123"/><hi type="bold">5. Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them--</hi>A special blessing was promised to the Israelites on condition of their obedience to the divine law; and this promise was remarkably verified at particular eras of their history, when pure and undefiled religion prevailed among them, in the public prosperity and domestic happiness enjoyed by them as a people. Obedience to the divine law always, indeed, ensures temporal advantages; and this, doubtless, was the primary meaning of the words, "which if a man do, he shall live in them." But that they had a higher reference to spiritual life is evident from the application made of them by our Lord (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.28">Lu 10:28</reference>) and the apostle (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">Ro 10:2</reference>). <div eID="gen1541" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c358f2cbffd1008dda4ff10d782bf8281ced8be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1124"/><div sID="gen1542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1124"/><hi type="bold">6. None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him--</hi>Very great laxity prevailed amongst the Egyptians in their sentiments and practice about the conjugal relation, as they not only openly sanctioned marriages between brothers and sisters, but even between parents and children. Such incestuous alliances Moses wisely prohibited, and his laws form the basis upon which the marriage regulations of this and other Christian nations are chiefly founded. This verse contains a general summary of all the particular prohibitions; and the forbidden intercourse is pointed out by the phrase, "to approach to." In the specified prohibitions that follow, all of which are included in this general summary, the prohibited familiarity is indicated by the phrases, to "uncover the nakedness" [Le 18:12-17], to "take" [Le 18:17, 18], and to "lie with" [Le 18:22, 23]. The phrase in this sixth verse, therefore, has the same identical meaning with each of the other three, and the marriages in reference to which it is used are those of consanguinity or too close affinity, amounting to incestuous connections. <div eID="gen1542" type="x-p"/>
entries.853b85c8e24c303d8f207893ccdf57aa2fbc0065: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1125"/><div sID="gen1543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1125"/><hi type="bold">18. Neither shalt thou take a wife to her sister, to vex her--</hi>The original is rendered in the Margin, "neither shalt thou take one wife to another to vex her," and two different and opposite interpretations have been put upon this passage. The marginal construction involves an express prohibition of polygamy; and, indeed, there can be no doubt that the practice of having more wives than one is directly contrary to the divine will. It was prohibited by the original law of marriage, and no evidence of its lawfulness under the Levitical code can be discovered, although Moses--from "the hardness of their hearts" [Mt 19:8; Mr 10:5]--tolerated it in the people of a rude and early age. The second interpretation forms the ground upon which the "vexed question" has been raised in our times respecting the lawfulness of marriage with a deceased wife's sister. Whatever arguments may be used to prove the unlawfulness or inexpediency of such a matrimonial relation, the passage under consideration cannot, on a sound basis of criticism, be enlisted in the service; for the crimes with which it is here associated warrant the conclusion that it points not to marriage with a deceased wife's sister, but with a sister in the wife's lifetime, a practice common among the ancient Egyptians, Chaldeans, and others. <div eID="gen1543" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f8578bf11ba647e05d256fdf7cc95760167017d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1126"/><div sID="gen1544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1126"/><hi type="bold">21. thou shalt not let any of thy seed pass through the fire to Molech, &c.--</hi>Molech, or Moloch, which signifies "king," was the idol of the Ammonites. His statue was of brass, and rested on a pedestal or throne of the same metal. His head, resembling that of a calf, was adorned with a crown, and his arms were extended in the attitude of embracing those who approached him. His devotees dedicated their children to him; and when this was to be done, they heated the statue to a high pitch of intensity by a fire within, and then the infants were either shaken over the flames, or passed through the ignited arms, by way of lustration to ensure the favor of the pretended deity. The fire-worshippers asserted that all children who did not undergo this purifying process would die in infancy; and the influence of this Zabian superstition was still so extensively prevalent in the days of Moses, that the divine lawgiver judged it necessary to prohibit it by an express statute.<div eID="gen1544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God--</hi>by giving it to false or pretended divinities; or, perhaps, from this precept standing in close connection with the worship of Molech, the meaning rather is, Do not, by devoting your children to him, give foreigners occasion to blaspheme the name of your God as a cruel and sanguinary deity, who demands the sacrifice of human victims, and who encourages cruelty in his votaries. <div eID="gen1545" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0eeface52ac72872dacb7af3cf4cfc7a014621b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1127"/><div sID="gen1546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1127"/><hi type="bold">24. Defile not yourselves in any of these things--</hi>In the preceding verses seventeen express cases of incest are enumerated; comprehending eleven of affinity [Le 18:7-16], and six of consanguinity [Le 18:17-20], together with some criminal enormities of an aggravated and unnatural character. In such prohibitions it was necessary for the instruction of a people low in the scale of moral perception, that the enumeration should be very specific as well as minute; and then, on completing it, the divine lawgiver announces his own views of these crimes, without any exception or modification, in the remarkable terms employed in this verse.<div eID="gen1546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all these the nations are defiled which I cast out before you, &c.--</hi>Ancient history gives many appalling proofs that the enormous vices described in this chapter were very prevalent, nay, were regularly practised from religious motives in the temples of Egypt and the groves of Canaan; and it was these gigantic social disorders that occasioned the expulsion, of which the Israelites were, in the hands of a righteous and retributive Providence, the appointed instruments (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Ge 15:16</reference>). The strongly figurative language of "the land itself vomiting out her inhabitants" [Le 18:25], shows the hopeless depth of their moral corruption. <div eID="gen1547" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8feaa4ebebc99db8ae6a7ef2883e1a3f8fa7f4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1128"/><div sID="gen1548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1128"/><hi type="bold">25. therefore I do visit the iniquity thereof upon it; and the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants--</hi>The Canaanites, as enormous and incorrigible sinners, were to be exterminated; and this extermination was manifestly a judicial punishment inflicted by a ruler whose laws had been grossly and perseveringly outraged. But before a law can be disobeyed, it must have been previously in existence; and hence a law, prohibiting all the horrid crimes enumerated above--a law obligatory upon the Canaanites as well as other nations--was already known and in force before the Levitical law of incest was promulgated. Some general Iaw, then, prohibiting these crimes must have been published to mankind at a very early period of the world's history; and that law must either have been the moral law, originally written on the human heart, or a law on the institution of marriage revealed to Adam and known to the Canaanites and others by tradition or otherwise. <div eID="gen1548" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2e1da3afe59a0bef91133fa727ee91623d2627c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1129"/><div sID="gen1549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1129"/><hi type="bold">29. the souls that commit them shall be cut off--</hi>This strong denunciatory language is applied to all the crimes specified in the chapter without distinction: to incest as truly as to bestiality, and to the eleven cases of affinity [Le 18:7-16], as fully as to the six of consanguinity [Le 18:17-20]. Death is the punishment sternly denounced against all of them. No language could be more explicit or universal; none could more strongly indicate intense loathing and abhorrence. <div eID="gen1549" type="x-p"/>
entries.e420e657535b801ebbf4fd1d392c1ec2e1153166: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1130"/><div sID="gen1550" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1130"/><hi type="bold">30. Therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance, that ye commit not any one of these abominable customs--</hi>In giving the Israelites these particular institutions, God was only re-delivering the law imprinted on the natural heart of man; for there is every reason to believe that the incestuous alliances and unnatural crimes prohibited in this chapter were forbidden to all men by a law expressed or understood from the beginning of the world, or at least from the era of the flood, since God threatens to condemn and punish, in a manner so sternly severe, these atrocities in the practice of the Canaanites and their neighbors, who were not subject to the laws of the Hebrew nation. <chapter eID="Lev.18"/>

entries.f448063af1294fab79208b2e2a7144bf661ce2d5: <div eID="gen4799" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4800" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4801" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4801" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4800" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4802" type="x-p"/> The people are commanded to avoid the doings of the Egyptians and Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.1-Lev.18.3">Lev 18:1-3</reference>. They are to do God's judgments, and to keep his ordinances, that they may live, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.4">Lev 18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Lev 18:5</reference>. Marriages with those who are near of kin are prohibited, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.6">Lev 18:6</reference>. None to marry with his mother or step-mother, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.7">Lev 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.8">Lev 18:8</reference>; with his sister or step-sister, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.9">Lev 18:9</reference>; with his grand-daughter, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.10">Lev 18:10</reference>; nor with the daughter of his step-mother, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.11">Lev 18:11</reference>; nor with his aunt, by father or mother, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.12">Lev 18:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.13">Lev 18:13</reference>; nor with his uncle's wife, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.14">Lev 18:14</reference>; nor with his daughter-in-law, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.15">Lev 18:15</reference>; nor sister-in-law, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.16">Lev 18:16</reference>; nor with a woman and her daughter, son's daughter, or daughter's daughter, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.17">Lev 18:17</reference>; nor with two sisters at the same time, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.18">Lev 18:18</reference>. Several abominations prohibited, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.19-Lev.18.23">Lev 18:19-23</reference>, of which the Canaanites, etc., were guilty, and for which they were cast out of the land, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.24">Lev 18:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.25">Lev 18:25</reference>. The people are exhorted to avoid these abominations, lest they be treated as the ancient inhabitants of the land were treated, and so cast out, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.26-Lev.18.28">Lev 18:26-28</reference>. Threatenings against the disobedient, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.29">Lev 18:29</reference>, and promises to the obedient, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.30">Lev 18:30</reference>.
entries.3e5e72a8c6983ae67b90b439ecf8ef98e8ba278c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4803" type="x-p"/> The doings of the land of Egypt - the land of Canaan - The worshipping of demons, beasts, etc., as mentioned in the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="Lev.17.7">Lev 17:7</reference>, and the abominations mentioned in this chapter from <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21-Lev.18.23">Lev 18:21-23</reference>.
entries.e6d3cd7cb496091c4164f9cafbfd2469fc07afa8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen4803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4804" type="x-p"/> Any that is near of kin - כל שאר בשרו col shear besaro, any remnant of his flesh, i.e., to any particularly allied to his own family, the prohibited degrees in which are specified from the 7th to the 17th verse (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.7-Lev.18.17">Lev 18:7-17</reference>) inclusive. Notwithstanding the prohibitions here, it must be evident that in the infancy of the world, persons very near of kin must have been joined in matrimonial alliances; and that even brothers must have matched with their own sisters. This must have been the case in the family of Adam. In these first instances necessity required this; when this necessity no longer existed, the thing became inexpedient and improper for two reasons: <div eID="gen4804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4805" type="x-p"/> 1. That the duties owing by nature to relatives might not be confounded with those of a social or political kind; for could a man be a brother and a husband, a son and a husband, at the same time, and fulfill the duties of both? Impossible. <div eID="gen4805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4806" type="x-p"/> 2. That by intermarrying with other families, the bonds of social compact might be strengthened and extended, so that the love of our neighbor, etc., might at once be felt to be not only a maxim of sound policy, but also a very practicable and easy duty; and thus feuds, divisions, and wars be prevented.
entries.081abc4e4ff854c678931571bddeb50436b7614b: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen4806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4807" type="x-p"/> Thy brother's wife - This was an illegal marriage, unless the brother died childless. In that case it was not only lawful for her to marry her brother-in-law, but he was obliged by the law, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.5">Deu 25:5</reference>, to take her to wife.
entries.da03bbd43c29aacf0a5865d109d99ef43558980b: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen4807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4808" type="x-p"/> A wife to her sister - Thou shalt not marry two sisters at the same time, as Jacob did Rachel and Leah; but there is nothing in this law that rendered it illegal to marry a sister-in-law when her sister was dead; therefore the text says, Thou shalt not take her in her life time, to vex her, alluding probably to the case of the jealousies and vexations which subsisted between Leah and Rachel, and by which the family peace was so often disturbed. Some think that the text may be so understood as also to forbid polygamy.
entries.9f5fa0bb5d9df8e331cde740bd764a6e68714cb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen4808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4809" type="x-p"/> As long as she is put apart - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.15.24">Lev 15:24</reference>.
entries.daf36b004fabe81db5e7c3b61cc1442b82998a2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen4809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4810" type="x-p"/> Thy neighbor's wife - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.20.14">Exo 20:14</reference>.
entries.473aedfcfad3b45617785cb69b19be7814050e66: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen4810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4811" type="x-p"/> Pass through the fire to Molech - The name of this idol is mentioned for the first time in this place. As the word מלח molech or melech signifies king or governor, it is very likely that this idol represented the sun; and more particularly as the fire appears to have been so much employed in his worship. There are several opinions concerning the meaning of passing through the fire to Molech. <div eID="gen4811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4812" type="x-p"/> 1. Some think that the semen humanum was offered on the fire to this idol. <div eID="gen4812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4813" type="x-p"/> 2. Others think that the children were actually made a burnt-offering to him. <div eID="gen4813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4814" type="x-p"/> 3. But others suppose the children were not burnt, but only passed through the fire, or between two fires, by way of consecration to him. <div eID="gen4814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4815" type="x-p"/> That some were actually burnt alive to this idol several scriptures, according to the opinion of commentators, seem strongly to intimate; see among others, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.38">Psa 106:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">Jer 7:31</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eze.23.37-Eze.23.39">Eze 23:37-39</reference>. That others were only consecrated to his service by passing between two fires the rabbins strongly assert; and if Ahaz had but one son, Hezekiah, (though it is probable he had others, see <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.3">2Chr 28:3</reference>), he is said to have passed through the fire to Molech, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.3">2Kgs 16:3</reference>, yet he succeeded his father in the kingdom, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.1">2Kgs 18:1</reference>, therefore this could only be a consecration, his idolatrous father intending thereby to initiate him early into the service of this demon. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.20.2">Lev 20:2</reference>.
entries.397c64ab0affd3ca261961fb4201e1e59fa9a541: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen4815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4816" type="x-p"/> With mankind - This abominable crime, frequent among the Greeks and Romans as well as the Canaanites, may be punished with death in this country.
entries.c8e1c1eda838a183f05c8554e514a16d7b0bd302: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen4816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4817" type="x-p"/> With any beast - This abomination is also punishable with death by the laws of this country. Any woman stand before a beast - That this was often done in Egypt there can be no doubt; and we have already seen, from the testimony of Herodotus, that a fact of this kind actually took place while he was in Egypt. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.17.7">Lev 17:7</reference>, and See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Lev.20.16">Lev 20:16</reference> (note).
entries.dcca40fbbdaa47e1a3b2490b957a0300c2b6fcf8: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen4817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4818" type="x-p"/> The land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants - This is a very nervous prosopopoeia or personification; a figure by which any part of inanimate nature may be represented as possessing the passions and reason of man. Here the land is represented as an intelligent being, with a deep and refined sense of moral good and evil: information concerning the abominations of the people is brought to this personified land, with which it is so deeply affected that a nausea is produced, and it vomits out its abominable and accursed inhabitants. It was natural for the inspired penman to make use of such a figure, as the description he was obliged to give of so many and enormous abominations must have affected him nearly in the same way in which he represents the land to be affected.
entries.207b1f78edc6c22bf620ad542187086ceea69f94: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen4818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4819" type="x-p"/> Shall ye keep mine ordinance - The only way to be preserved from all false worship is seriously to consider and devoutly to observe the ordinances of the true religion. He who in the things of God goes no farther than he can say, Thus it is written, and thus it behoves me to do, is never likely to receive a false creed, nor perform a superstitious act of worship. <div eID="gen4819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4820" type="x-p"/> 1. How true is that word, The law of the Lord is Perfect! In a small compass, and in a most minute detail, it comprises every thing that is calculated to instruct, direct, convince, correct, and fortify the mind of man. Whatever has a tendency to corrupt or injure man, that it forbids; whatever is calculated to comfort him, promote and secure his best interests, that it commands. It takes him in all possible states, views him in all connections, and provides for his present and eternal happiness. <div eID="gen4820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4821" type="x-p"/> 2. As the human soul is polluted and tends to pollution, the great doctrine of the law is holiness to the Lord: this it keeps invariably in view in all its commands, precepts, ordinances, rites, and ceremonies. And how forcibly in all these does it say, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength; and thy neighbor as thyself! This is the prominent doctrine of the preceding chapter; and this shall be fulfilled in all them who believe, for Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to them that believe. <div eID="gen4821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4822" type="x-p"/> Reader, magnify God for his law, for by it is the knowledge of sin; and magnify him for his Gospel, for by this is the cure of sin. Let the law be thy schoolmaster to bring thee to Christ, that thou mayest be justified by faith; and that the righteousness of the law may be fulfilled in thee, and that thou mayest walk, not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.  <chapter eID="Lev.18"/> <div eID="gen4822" type="x-p"/>

entries.fad3a4c2622c5a033943b7c9c2d9bd3b64f47234: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.1-Lev.18.4">Lev 18:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen1380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1381" type="x-p"/> By the words, “I am Jehovah your God,” which are placed at the head and repeated at the close (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.30">Lev 18:30</reference>), the observance of the command is enforced upon the people as a covenant obligation, and urged upon them most strongly by the promise, that through the observance of the ordinances and judgments of Jehovah they should live (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Lev 18:5</reference>).
entries.1694e8dbaf05d43f81e3a1f4503bb942d0fd83bc: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Lev 18:5</reference> <div eID="gen1381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1382" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The man who does them</hi> (the ordinances of Jehovah) <hi type="italic">shall live</hi> (gain true life) <hi type="italic">through them</hi>” (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.1.16">Exo 1:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.3.22">Gen 3:22</reference>).
entries.f3e7fabae9cd06b315cf3ed3404e7663e686b2e6: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.6-Lev.18.7">Lev 18:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen1382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1383" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">laws against incest</hi> are introduced in <reference osisRef="Lev.18.6">Lev 18:6</reference> with the general prohibition, descriptive of the nature of this sin, “None of you shall approach בּשׂרו אל־כּל־שׁאר to any flesh of his flesh, to uncover nakedness.” The difference between שׁאר flesh, and בּשׂר flesh, is involved in obscurity, as both words are used in connection with edible flesh (see the Lexicons). “Flesh of his flesh” is a flesh that is of his own flesh, belongs to the same flesh as himself (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.24">Gen 2:24</reference>), and is applied to a blood-relation, blood-relationship being called שׁארה (or flesh-kindred) in Hebrew (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.17">Lev 18:17</reference>). Sexual intercourse is called uncovering the nakedness of another (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.36">Eze 16:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.18">Eze 23:18</reference>). The prohibition relates to both married and unmarried intercourse, though the reference is chiefly to the former (see <reference osisRef="Lev.18.18">Lev 18:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.14">Lev 20:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.17">Lev 20:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.21">Lev 20:21</reference>). Intercourse is forbidden (1) with a mother, (2) with a step-mother, (3) with a sister or half-sister, (4) with a granddaughter, the daughter of either son or daughter, (5) with the daughter of a step-mother, (6) with an aunt, the sister of either father or mother, (7) with the wife of an uncle on the father’s side, (8) with a daughter-in-law, (9) with a sister-in-law, or brother’s wife, (10) with a woman and her daughter, or a woman and her granddaughter, and (11) with two sisters at the same time. No special reference is made to sexual intercourse with (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) a daughter, (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) a full sister, (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) a mother-in-law; the last, however, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.27.23">Deu 27:23</reference> as an accursed crime, is included here in No. 10, and the second in No. 3, whilst the first, like parricide in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.15">Exo 21:15</reference>, is not expressly noticed, simply because the crime was regarded as one that never could occur. Those mentioned under Nos. 1, 2, 3, 8, and 10 were to be followed by the death or extermination of the criminals (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.11-Lev.20.12">Lev 20:11-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.14">Lev 20:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.17">Lev 20:17</reference>), on account of their being accursed crimes (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.1">Deu 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.20">Deu 27:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.22-Deut.27.23">Deu 27:22-23</reference>). On the other hand, the only threat held out in the case of the connection mentioned under Nos. 6, 7, and 9, was that those who committed such crimes should bear their iniquity, or die childless (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.19-Lev.20.21">Lev 20:19-21</reference>). The cases noticed under Nos. 4 and 5 are passed over in ch. 20, though they no doubt belonged to the crimes which were to be punished with death, and No. 11, for which no punishment was fixed, because the wrong had been already pointed out in Lev 18:18.<note placement="foot">The marriage laws and customs were much more lax among the Gentiles. With the Egyptians it was lawful to marry sisters and half-sisters (<hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> i. 27), and the licentiousness of the women was very great among them (see at Gen 39:6.). With the Persians marriage was allowed with mother, daughter, and sister (<hi type="italic">Clem. Al. strom.</hi> iii. p. 431;<hi type="italic">Eusebii praep. ev.</hi> vi. 10); and this is also said to have been the case with the Medians, Indians, and Ethiopians, as well as with the Assyrians (<hi type="italic">Jerome adv. Jovin</hi>. ii. 7; <hi type="italic">Lucian, Sacriff</hi>. 5); whereas the Greeks and Romans abhorred such marriages, and the Athenians and Spartans only permitted marriages with half-sisters (cf. <hi type="italic">Selden de jure nat. et gent</hi>. v. 11, pp. 619ff.). The ancient Arabs, before the time of Mohammed, were very strict in this respect, and would not allow of marriage with a mother, daughter, or aunt on either the father’s or mother’s side, or with two sisters at the same time. The only cases on record of marriage between brothers and sisters are among the Arabs of Marbat (<hi type="italic">Seetzen, Zach’s Mon. Corresp.</hi> Oct. 1809). This custom Mohammed raised into a law, and extended it to nieces, nurses, foster-sisters, etc. (<hi type="italic">Koran, Sure</hi> iv. 20ff.).</note> <div eID="gen1383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1384" type="x-p"/> Elaborate commentaries upon this chapter are to be found in <hi type="italic">Michaelis Abhandl. über die Ehegesetze Mosis,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">Mos. Recht;</hi> also in <hi type="italic">Saalschütz Mos. Recth.</hi> See also my <hi type="italic">Archäologie</hi> ii. p. 108. For the rabbinical laws and those of the Talmud, see <hi type="italic">Selden oxur ebr.</hi> lib. 1, c. 1ff., and <hi type="italic">Saalschütz ut sup</hi>. <div eID="gen1384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1385" type="x-p"/> The enumeration of the different cases commences in <reference osisRef="Lev.18.7">Lev 18:7</reference> very appropriately with the prohibition of incest with a mother. Sexual connection with a mother is called “uncovering the nakedness of father and mother.” As husband and wife are one flesh (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.24">Gen 2:24</reference>), the nakedness of the husband is uncovered in that of his wife, or, as it is described in <reference osisRef="Deut.22.30">Deu 22:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.20">Deu 27:20</reference>, the wing, i.e., the edge, of the bedclothes of the father’s bed, as the husband spreads his bedclothes over his wife as well as himself (Rth 3:9). For, strictly speaking, ערוה גּלּה is only used with reference to the wife; but in the dishonouring of his wife the honour of the husband is violated also, and his bed defiled, Gen 49:4. It is wrong, therefore, to interpret the verse, as <hi type="italic">Jonathan</hi> and <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> do, as relating to carnal intercourse between a daughter and father. Not only is this at variance with the circumstance that all these laws are intended for the man alone, and addressed expressly to him, but also with <reference osisRef="Lev.18.8">Lev 18:8</reference>, where the nakedness of the father’s wife is distinctly called the father’s shame.
entries.c42cc32cba9e6fbcd81824eecd1c3576987e9d87: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.8">Lev 18:8</reference> <div eID="gen1385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1386" type="x-p"/> Intercourse with a father’s wife, i.e., with a step-mother, is forbidden as uncovering the father’s nakedness; since a father’s wife stood in blood-relationship only to the son whose mother she was. But for the father’s sake her nakedness was to be inaccessible to the son, and uncovering it was to be punished with death as incest (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.11">Lev 20:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.20">Deu 27:20</reference>). By the “father’s wife” we are probably to understand not merely his full lawful wife, but his concubine also, since the father’s bed was defiled in the latter case no less than in the former (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">Gen 49:4</reference>), and an accursed crime was committed, the punishment of which was death. At all events, it cannot be inferred from <reference osisRef="Lev.19.20-Lev.19.22">Lev 19:20-22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.21.9">Exo 21:9</reference>, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes, that a milder punishment was inflicted in this case.
entries.f7eb5cd1315e86fee2999412cc70cf814e624932: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.9">Lev 18:9</reference> <div eID="gen1386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1387" type="x-p"/> By the sister, the daughter of father or mother, we are to understand only the step-or half-sister, who had either the same father or the same mother as the brother had. The clause, “<hi type="italic">whether born at home or born abroad,</hi>” does not refer to legitimate or illegitimate birth, but is to be taken as a more precise definition of the words, daughter of thy father or of thy mother, and understood, as <hi type="italic">Lud. de Dieu</hi> supposes, as referring to the half-sister “of the first marriage, whether the father’s daughter left by a deceased wife, or the mother’s daughter left by a deceased husband,” so that the person marrying her would be a son by a second marriage. Sexual intercourse with a half-sister is described as חסד in <reference osisRef="Lev.20.17">Lev 20:17</reference>, and threatened with extermination. This word generally signifies sparing love, favour, grace; but here, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.14.34">Pro 14:34</reference>, it means dishonour, shame, from the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> חסּד, to dishonour.
entries.ffb4ac5c6ee376db29e1afab48370c108b5c8ddd: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.10">Lev 18:10</reference> <div eID="gen1387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1388" type="x-p"/> The prohibition of marriage with a granddaughter, whether the daughter of a son or daughter, is explained in the words, “for they are thy nakedness,” the meaning of which is, that as they were directly descended from the grandfather, carnal intercourse with them would be equivalent to dishonouring his own flesh and blood.
entries.04c7a0e3f8d70c09a9592bebf070c361ad3ba82a: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.11">Lev 18:11</reference> <div eID="gen1388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1389" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The daughter of thy father’s wife</hi> (i.e., thy step-mother), <hi type="italic">born to thy father,</hi>” is the half-sister by a second marriage; and the prohibition refers to the son by a first marriage, whereas <reference osisRef="Lev.18.9">Lev 18:9</reference> treats of the son by a second marriage. The notion that the man’s own mother is also included, and that the prohibition includes marriage with a full sister, is at variance with the usage of the expression “thy father’s wife.”
entries.8921ceadc5e27d7265e6282993018e6a8e26106e: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.12-Lev.18.13">Lev 18:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen1389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1390" type="x-p"/> Marriage or conjugal intercourse with the sister of either father or mother (i.e., with either the paternal or maternal aunt) was prohibited, because she was the blood-relation of the father or mother. שׁאר = בּשׂר שׁאר (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.6">Lev 18:6</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.20.19">Lev 20:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.21.2">Lev 21:2</reference>; Num 27:11), hence שׁארה, blood-relationship (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.17">Lev 18:17</reference>).
entries.492d124cca511db5c20c52a082abccd6eb5532dc: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.14">Lev 18:14</reference> <div eID="gen1390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1391" type="x-p"/> So, again, with the wife of the father’s brother, because the nakedness of the uncle was thereby uncovered. The threat held out in <reference osisRef="Lev.20.19">Lev 20:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.20.20">Lev 20:20</reference> against the alliances prohibited in <reference osisRef="Lev.18.12-Lev.18.14">Lev 18:12-14</reference>, is that the persons concerned should bear their iniquity or sin, i.e., should suffer punishment in consequence (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Lev 5:1</reference>); and in the last case it is stated that they should die childless. From this it is obvious that sexual connection with the sister of either father or mother was not to be punished with death by the magistrate, but would be punished with disease by God Himself.
entries.7a910facd143e6f2603098d72fa54165dba0cb0d: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.15">Lev 18:15</reference> <div eID="gen1391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1392" type="x-p"/> Sexual connection with a daughter-in-law, a son’s wife, is called תּבל in <reference osisRef="Lev.20.12">Lev 20:12</reference>, and threatened with death to both the parties concerned. תּבל, from בּלל to mix, to confuse, signifies a sinful mixing up or confusing of the divine ordinances by unnatural unchastity, like the lying of a woman with a beast, which is the only other connection in which the word occurs (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.23">Lev 18:23</reference>).
entries.d9aabaec899ec166decb09117ef688614cdbcb39: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.16">Lev 18:16</reference> <div eID="gen1392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1393" type="x-p"/> Marriage with a brother’s wife was a sin against the brother’s nakedness, a sexual defilement, which God would punish with barrenness. This prohibition, however, only refers to cases in which the deceased brother had left children; for if he had died childless, the brother not only might, but was required to marry his sister-in-law (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.5">Deu 25:5</reference>).
entries.f97df54ef04759919c61dfb746d19bbc8b8fc170: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.17">Lev 18:17</reference> <div eID="gen1393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1394" type="x-p"/> Marriage with a woman and her daughter, whether both together or in succession, is described in <reference osisRef="Deut.27.20">Deu 27:20</reference> as an accursed lying with the mother-in-law; whereas here it is the relation to the step-daughter which is primarily referred to, as we may see from the parallel prohibition, which is added, against taking the daughter of her son or daughter, i.e., the granddaughter-in-law. Both of these were crimes against blood-relationship which were to be punished with death in the case of both parties (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.14">Lev 20:14</reference>), because they were “wickedness,” זמּה, lit., invention, design, here applied to the crime of licentiousness and whoredom (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.29">Lev 19:29</reference>; Jdg 20:6; <reference osisRef="Job.31.11">Job 31:11</reference>).
entries.c51de7483d4cb1b116c03437c332094c47e3a5d5: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.18">Lev 18:18</reference> <div eID="gen1394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1395" type="x-p"/> Lastly, it was forbidden to take a wife to her sister (עליה upon her, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.28.9">Gen 28:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.31.50">Gen 31:50</reference>) in her life-time, that is to say, to marry two sisters at the same time, לצרר “to pack together, to uncover this nakedness,” i.e., to pack both together into one marriage bond, and so place the sisters in carnal union through their common husband, and disturb the sisterly relation, as the marriage with two sisters that was forced upon Jacob had evidently done. No punishment is fixed for the marriage with two sisters; and, of course, after the death of the first wife a man was at liberty to marry her sister.<hi type="italic">Prohibition of other kinds of unchastity and of unnatural crimes</hi>. - <reference osisRef="Lev.18.19">Lev 18:19</reference> prohibits intercourse with a woman during her uncleanness. טמאה נדּת signifies the uncleanness of a woman’s hemorrhage, whether menstruation or after childbirth, which is called in <reference osisRef="Lev.12.7">Lev 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.18">Lev 20:18</reference>, the fountain of bleeding. The guilty persons were both of them to be cut off from their nation according to <reference osisRef="Lev.20.18">Lev 20:18</reference>, i.e., to be punished with death.
entries.1b1efa9c6992540127c5cbd53a19e2bdffdf18e6: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.20">Lev 18:20</reference> “To a neighbour’s wife thou shalt not give שׁכבתּך thy pouring as seed” (i.e., make her pregnant), “to defile thyself with her,” viz., by the <hi type="italic">emissio seminis</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.16-Lev.15.17">Lev 15:16-17</reference>), a defilement which was to be punished as adultery by the stoning to death of both parties (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.10">Lev 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.22.22">Deu 22:22</reference>, cf. Joh 9:5).
entries.fff794b2162f99e285342926d218ef78e66f6e79: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Lev 18:21</reference> <div eID="gen1395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1396" type="x-p"/> To bodily unchastity there is appended a prohibition of spiritual whoredom. “<hi type="italic">Thou shalt not give of thy seed to cause to pass through</hi> (sc., the fire; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">Deu 18:10</reference>) <hi type="italic">for Moloch</hi>.” המּלך is constantly written with the article: it is rendered by the lxx ἄρχων both here and in Lev 20:2., but ὁ Μολόχ βασιλεύς in other places (2Ki 23:10; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.35">Jer 32:35</reference>). <hi type="italic">Moloch</hi> was an old Canaanitish idol, called by the Phoenicians and Carthaginians <hi type="italic">Melkarth, Baal-melech, Malcom,</hi> and other such names, and related to Baal, a sun-god worshipped, like <hi type="italic">Kronos</hi> and <hi type="italic">Saturn</hi>, by the sacrifice of children. It was represented by a brazen statue, which was hollow and capable of being heated, and formed with a bull’s head, and arms stretched out to receive the children to be sacrificed. From the time of Ahaz children were slain at Jerusalem in the valley of Ben-hinnom, and then sacrificed by being laid in the heated arms and burned (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.20-Ezek.16.21">Eze 16:20-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.35">Jer 32:35</reference>; 2Ki 23:10; 2Ki 16:3; 2Ki 17:17; 2Ki 21:6, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.37-Ps.106.38">Psa 106:37-38</reference>). Now although this offering of children in the valley of Ben-hinnom is called a “slaughtering” by Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.21">Eze 16:21</reference>), and a “burning through (in the) fire” by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">Jer 7:31</reference>), and although, in the times of the later kings, children were actually given up to Moloch and burned as slain-offerings, even among the Israelites; it by no means follows from this, that “passing through to Moloch,” or “passing through the fire,” or “passing through the fire to Moloch” (2Ki 23:10), signified slaughtering and burning with fire, though this has been almost unanimously assumed since the time of <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi>. But according to the unanimous explanation of the Rabbins, fathers, and earlier theologians, “causing to pass through the fire” denoted primarily going through the fire without burning, a februation, or purification through fire, by which the children were consecrated to Moloch; a kind of fire-baptism, which preceded the sacrificing, and was performed, particularly in olden time, without actual sacrificing, or slaying and burning. For februation was practised among the most different nations without being connected with human sacrifices; and, like most of the idolatrous rites of the heathen, no doubt the worship of Moloch assumed different forms at different times and among different nations. If the Israelites had really sacrificed their children to Moloch, i.e., had slain and burned them, before the time of Ahaz, the burning would certainly have been mentioned before; for Solomon had built a high place upon the mountain to the east of Jerusalem for Moloch, the abomination of the children of Ammon, to please his foreign wives (1Ki 11:7 : see the Art. Moloch in <hi type="italic">Herzog's</hi> Cycl.). This idolatrous worship was to be punished with death by stoning, as a desecration of the name of Jehovah, and a defiling of His sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.3">Lev 20:3</reference>), i.e., as a practical contempt of the manifestations of the grace of the living God (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.2-Lev.20.3">Lev 20:2-3</reference>).
entries.4fa9ec399c2250142bd7e60cc50f34e4895414af: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.22-Lev.18.23">Lev 18:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen1396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1397" type="x-p"/> Lastly, it was forbidden to “lie with mankind as with womankind,” i.e., to commit the crime of <hi type="italic">paederastia</hi>, that sin of Sodom (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.5">Gen 19:5</reference>), to which the whole of the heathen were more or less addicted (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.27">Rom 1:27</reference>), and from which even the Israelites did not keep themselves free (Jdg 19:22.); or to “lie with any beast.” “Into no beast shalt thou give thine emission of seed,...and a woman shall not place herself before a beast to lie down thereto.” רבע = רבץ “to lie,” is the term used particularly to denote a crime of this description (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.13">Lev 20:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.20.15">Lev 20:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.16">Lev 20:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.22.18">Exo 22:18</reference>). Lying with animals was connected in Egypt with the worship of the goat; at Mendes especially, where the women lay down before he-goats (<hi type="italic">Herodotus</hi>, 2, 46; <hi type="italic">Strabo</hi>, 17, p. 802). Aelian (nat. an. vii. 19) relates an account of the crime being also committed with a dog in Rome; and according to <hi type="italic">Sonnini</hi>, R. 11, p. 330, in modern Egypt men are said to lie even with female crocodiles.
entries.99a11be50dcf0b9b45c60dd5b582af141bd46b54: <reference osisRef="Lev.18.24-Lev.18.30">Lev 18:24-30</reference> <div eID="gen1397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1398" type="x-p"/> In the concluding exhortation God pointed expressly to the fact, that the nations which He was driving out before the Israelites (the participle משׁלּח is used of that which is certainly and speedily coming to pass) had defiled the land by such abominations as those, that He had visited their iniquity and the land had spat out its inhabitants, and warned the Israelites to beware of these abominations, that the land might not spit them out as it had the Canaanites before them. The pret. ותּקא (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.25">Lev 18:25</reference>) and קאה (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">Lev 18:28</reference>) are prophetic (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.20.22-Lev.20.23">Lev 20:22-23</reference>), and the expression is poetical. The land is personified as a living creature, which violently rejects food that it dislikes. “<hi type="italic">Hoc enim tropo vult significare Scriptura enormitatem criminum, quod scilicet ipsae creaturae irrationales suo creatori semper obedientes et pro illo pugnantes detestentur peccatores tales eosque terra quasi evomat, cum illi expelluntur ab ea</hi>” (<hi type="italic">C. a Lap.</hi>).  <chapter eID="Lev.18"/> <div eID="gen1398" type="x-p"/>

entries.4b9a651dab634b7cf128d2eda926fd8b783261c8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.18.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.18.1" sID="gen15309" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen15310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1. </hi><hi type="italic">And the Lord spoke unto Moses</hi>. I have not introduced this declaration amongst other similar ones, which had for their object the preparation of their minds for the reverent reception of the Law, because, whatever conformity there may be in the words themselves, in their substance there is a great difference; for they were general, whereas this is specially confined to a single point. For it was not God’s intention here merely to exhort the people to the study of the Law, but the address respecting the keeping of His statutes is directed to the present cause, since He does not refer indifferently to all the statutes of Himself and of the Gentiles, but restricts Himself to the subject-matter, as it is called; and thus, by the statutes of the Gentiles, He means those corruptions whereby they had perverted His pure institution as to holy matrimony. First, however, tie forbids them from following the customs of the Egyptians, and then includes all the Canaanitish nations. For, since all the Orientals are libidinous, they never had any scruple in polluting themselves by incestuous marriages; whilst it is abundantly proved by history, how great were the excesses of the Egyptians <note n="86"> <div sID="gen15311" type="x-p"/> “A very objectionable custom, which is not only noticed by Diodorus, but is fully authenticated by the sculptures both of Upper and Lower Egypt, existed among them from the earliest times, the origin and policy of which it is not easy to explain — the marriage of brother and sister, which Diodorus supposes to have been owing to, and sanctioned by, that of His and Osiris; but as this was purely an allegorical fable, and these ideal personages never lived on earth, his conjecture is of little weight; nor does any ancient writer offer a satisfactory explanation of so strange a custom.” — Wilkinson’s Popular Account of the Ancient Egyptians, 2:224.<div eID="gen15311" type="x-p"/> </note> in this respect. A brother had no abhorrence against marrying his uterine sister, nor a paternal or maternal uncle his niece; in a word, they were so dead to. shame that they were carried away by their lusts to trample upon all the laws of nature. This is the reason why God here enumerates the kinds of incest of which the mention would else have been superfluous.<div eID="gen15310" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.18.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15309" osisID="Lev.18.1" type="section"/>
entries.8a1df533bfcd76c96c227bfc65e81252bce1c226: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.18.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.18.4" sID="gen15312" type="section"/> <div sID="gen15313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4. </hi><hi type="italic">Ye shall therefore keep my statutes and my judgments</hi>. Because it is no less difficult to correct vices, to which men have been long accustomed, than to cure diseases of long standing, especially because people in general so pertinaciously cleave to bad examples, God adduces His statutes, in order to recall the people from the errors of their evil habits into the right way. For nothing is more absurd than for us to fix our minds on the actions of men, and not on God’s word, in which is to be found the rule of a holy life. It is, therefore, just as if God would overthrow whatever had been received from long custom, and abolish the universal consent of the world by the authority of His doctrine. With this object He commands His Law to be regarded not once only, as we have already seen, lest the Israelites should abandon themselves to filthy lusts; but He diligently inculcates upon them, that they should turn away from all abuses, and keep themselves within the bounds and ordinances of His Law. And to this refers the expression, “I am the Lord your God;” containing a comparison between Himself and the heathen nations, between whom and His people He had interposed, as it were, a wall of partition.<div eID="gen15313" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.18.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15312" osisID="Lev.18.4" type="section"/>
entries.f0da2a30a3fd7a2ae013aba81f73c3c4a26423aa:
5. Ye shall therefore keep my statutes.
